question: How is rehabilitation different from acute care?

options.A: Managing sudden spikes in vital signs
options.C: Curing the underlying acute infectious disease
options.D: Achieving maximum independence and quality of life

explanation: Acute care fixes the sudden emergency, but rehab is all about helping your patient get back on their feet and live life to the fullest over the long haul. You've got this!

question: What makes the rehabilitation nurse's role so special compared to a regular hospital nurse?

options.A: Nurses work completely in isolation without consulting other health professionals
options.B: It only involves administering intravenous medications on a strict schedule
options.C: It focuses heavily on helping clients adapt to long-term changes rather than just curing them
options.D: It completely replaces the need for physical and occupational therapy

explanation: Rehab nursing is less about quick fixes and more about walking side-by-side with patients as they adjust to long-term changes. Great nursing is heart work!

question: What does having an 'ability-focused mindset' mean for the healthcare team?

options.A: What the client is still able to do
options.B: The permanent deficits caused by the injury
options.C: How fast the client can be discharged home

explanation: Instead of focusing on what a patient has lost, an ability-focused mindset looks at their remaining strengths to build their confidence. Spotting strengths is a great nursing skill!

question: How does a nurse show client-centered care when planning a patient's rehab?

options.A: Involving the client and family in setting realistic daily personal goals
options.B: Following a rigid hospital routine without considering individual preferences
options.C: Deciding the discharge schedule without asking the client about their home setup
options.D: Focusing solely on physical therapy exercises prescribed by the doctor

explanation: Client-centered care means the patient and their family are part of the team, not just bystanders. When goals matter to them, they work harder to reach them!

question: In SMART goal setting for rehab, what does the letter 'M' stand for?
explanation: 'M' stands for measurable! It means you can actually track progress and see how far your patient has come. Easy peasy!

question: Why do we break long-term rehab down into small, bite-sized goals?

options.A: They eliminate the need for any further nursing assessments
options.B: They guarantee that the patient will be discharged within forty-eight hours
options.C: They ensure the insurance company approves unlimited hospital stays
options.D: They prevent client frustration and help maintain motivation during a long recovery

explanation: Recovery can feel overwhelming. Small daily wins keep patients motivated and smiling instead of giving up. You're doing great!

question: Which rehab team member helps patients master everyday tasks like eating, bathing, and dressing?
explanation: Occupational therapists (OTs) are the masters of 'occupations'—meaning everyday living activities. They help patients get back to doing things for themselves!

question: What is the main job of the rehab nurse within the healthcare team?

options.A: Prescribing physical therapy exercises and ordering diagnostic imaging tests
options.B: Reinforcing therapy skills and coordinating daily care around the clock
options.C: Providing formal legal counseling for insurance claims
options.D: Performing major orthopedic surgeries to correct bone deformities

explanation: Nurses are with the patient 24/7. We tie all the therapies together and keep the healing going round the clock. You are the heartbeat of the ward!

question: Why shouldn't a nurse rush in and do everything for a slow-moving rehab patient?

options.A: It prevents the client from ever needing assistive devices
options.B: It saves nursing time during busy morning shifts
options.C: Doing it for them reduces their chance to practice and slows down their independence
options.D: Hospital policies strictly forbid nurses from helping with dressing

explanation: It's tough to watch them struggle, but letting them do it themselves builds muscle memory and true independence. Patience is a nurse's superpower!

question: What is the best nursing action to prevent joint stiffness (contractures) in a bedridden patient?

options.A: Keeping the client lying flat in bed in the exact same position all day
options.B: Restricting fluid intake to prevent bathroom trips
options.C: Performing regular passive and active range-of-motion exercises
options.D: Applying tight bandages around all four limbs

explanation: Regular range-of-motion keeps those joints moving and happy. If you don't move it, you lose it!

question: When is the best time to start planning for a patient's discharge home?

options.A: When the client asks to go home
options.B: After all therapy sessions have finished
options.C: Twenty-four hours before leaving the hospital

explanation: Discharge planning starts right from day one! That way, there's no last-minute panic when it's time to go home. Smart nursing!

question: Why does the healthcare team do a home assessment before a patient is discharged?

options.A: It helps identify physical barriers like stairs or narrow doors that could cause falls or limit mobility
options.B: It replaces the need for physical therapy sessions in the clinic
options.C: It proves to the doctor that the client no longer needs any assistance
options.D: It allows the hospital to bill the client for interior decorating services

explanation: Checking the home early helps spot hazards like steps or narrow doors so ramps or rails can be fitted before the patient arrives. Safety first!
